content: 1. Space Allocation and PPE Use: Designate specific areas for handling contaminated items and performing decontamination activities. Use light personal protective equipment (PPE) when handling clean medical devices. For contaminated items, full PPE is mandatory. 2. Cleaning Agents and Disinfectants: Identify available cleaning agents and disinfectants for decontaminating medical equipment. Suitable disinfectants include a 5% chlorine solution or 70% ethanol. Note that manufacturer guidelines may not specifically address Ebola virus decontamination; in such cases, use surrogate pathogens as a worst-case scenario for cleaning protocols. 3. Protection of Cleaned Equipment: 4. Decontamination of Medical Equipment: Follow specific standard operating procedures (SOPs) for decontaminating various categories of medical equipment: Non-electro-mechanical devices (e.g., tourniquets, measuring tapes): Clean thoroughly and disinfect with alcohol or chlorine solutions. Mechanical devices (e.g. Disassemble if possible, clean thoroughly, and disinfect. Electro-mechanical devices (e.g., ECG monitors, pulse oximeters): Remove batteries if applicable, clean, and disinfect carefully to avoid damage. Respiratory equipment (e.g., ventilators, oxygen concentrators): Disassemble, discard filters, clean, and disinfect thoroughly. 5. Disposables and Consumables: Single-use items without sharp edges (e.g., PPE, IV cannulas, catheters) should be disposed of immediately in sturdy, clearly labeled bags to prevent cross-contamination. Items with intact packaging may be redistributed or returned to donors. Single-use items with sharp edges (e.g., needles, syringes) must be disposed of in puncture-resistant, fluid-impermeable sharps containers and incinerated. 6. General Decontamination Steps: Use full PPE in high-risk areas (red zones) and lighter PPE in low-risk areas (green zones). If zones are not clearly distinguishable, full PPE should be worn at all times. Verify the cleaning process once implemented and cover cleaned devices in plastic to prevent accidental soiling. 7. Waste Management: Hazardous waste, including plastics, should be incinerated or deeply buried if incineration is not feasible. Metal and ceramic medical devices damaged beyond repair should also be buried. 8. Medication Disposal: Expired medications should be disposed of according to WHO or national guidelines, preferably through incineration. Non-expired, unopened medications stored under proper conditions may be redirected to other health facilities. 9. Laboratory Equipment Decontamination: Items used for Ebola testing should be sterilized using methods like steam autoclaving. Biosafety cabinets (BSCs) require fumigation and expert handling for decontamination. Decontaminate laboratory work surfaces with appropriate disinfectants and follow national procedures for disposing of expired chemicals. 10. Occupational Health and Safety: Provide adequate PPE, first aid kits, and training for workers. 11. Completion and Reporting: After decommissioning, confirm the site is safe and free of hazards. Document lessons learned for future operations. 12. Hydrated Lime Use: Hydrated lime can be used to reduce water content in septic tanks during decommissioning. By adhering to these detailed protocols, the decommissioning of Ebola care facilities can be conducted safely and effectively, minimizing risks to workers and the community.
